# Garry Kasparov: Career and Contributions
Garry Kasparov, born in 1963 in Baku, Azerbaijan, rose to fame as one of chess's greatest players. He began studying chess seriously as a child and trained under prominent Soviet coaches, winning the Soviet Junior Championships at ages 13 and 14. By age 15, Kasparov qualified for the USSR Chess Championship, marking him as the youngest player to reach that level. He became a grandmaster by 1980 and rapidly ascended the global ranks, winning the World Junior Chess Championship and earning a provisional rating that put him among the world’s top players. Kasparov became the youngest-ever world No. 1 in January 1984 and won the Candidates' final against Vasily Smyslov to earn a shot at the world championship.
Kasparov's reign as world champion began in 1985, defeating Anatoly Karpov and holding the title until 2000, after a series of famous and fiercely competitive matches against Karpov. He broke with FIDE in 1993, creating the Professional Chess Association and splitting the world title, but remained the dominant figure in chess, defending his title against strong challengers and maintaining an all-time high rating of 2851. Kasparov retired from professional chess in 2005 as the world’s top-ranked player, having set records for tournament victories, consecutive wins, and months as number one. He has since played exhibitions, coached elite players like Magnus Carlsen, authored influential chess books (including the "My Great Predecessors" series), and made significant theoretical contributions to chess openings and computer chess. Recognized for his dynamic, aggressive style, Kasparov is often cited as one of the greatest chess players in history.

# Political Activism, Writing, and Personal Life
Beyond chess, Kasparov became an outspoken advocate for democracy and human rights, particularly in Russia. He founded the United Civil Front, participated in protest movements against Vladimir Putin’s administration, and ran for president of Russia as the "Other Russia" coalition candidate in 2008, though his candidacy was stymied by barriers to participation. After facing persecution, he left Russia in 2013 and continued his activism in exile, criticizing Putin’s regime, supporting democratic reforms, and advocating for Russian opposition. Kasparov also speaks out on international affairs and artificial intelligence, has received Croatian citizenship for his work supporting Croatian independence, and served as chairman of the Human Rights Foundation until 2024.
Kasparov published numerous books on chess, strategy, and politics (notably "Winter Is Coming"), and contributed to documentaries and chess education. He has been married three times and has four children, currently residing in New York City since 2013.
